name: Interview behavioural questions, set 4
description: Spoken behavioural questions with rubrics: deadlines, feedback, a changed mind, research, hobbies, pressure, setbacks, offers, bugs and follow-ups. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you ran something with a deadline and not enough people.
widget.model: In my second year I ran our society's charity quiz night with too few people. Three weeks out, two of my five helpers left for exams. My job was to deliver the night for 120 guests and raise at least £1,500. First I listed every job and the hours it needed. It came to about 60 hours for three people, which was too much. So I cut what guests would not miss, such as printed menus and a raffle, saving ten hours. I asked two first-years to run the door for one evening each, with a one-page checklist. I kept the question writing myself and set my own draft deadline a week early. When the venue moved our booking by a day, that spare week absorbed it. On the night we hosted 130 guests and raised £1,840. I learned to cost the work in hours first, then cut scope before asking for more people.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: what you ran, the deadline and the shortfall
A specific situation: the scale, the deadline and what was at stake
Your own actions in the first person: how you planned, cut and handed out work
A number or concrete result, set against the target
A lesson about working short-handed, stated plainly
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows how you sized the work and chose what to cut. Interviewers want your own decisions, not the team's effort in general. End with the result against the target and one lesson.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you gave someone hard feedback.
widget.model: Last year I told a friend in my statistics project group that his work was holding us back. Our report was due in ten days, and his data section was a week late and thin. I needed to raise it without losing him from the team. I asked to meet him alone, not in the group chat. I started with what I had seen: two missed team deadlines, and 300 words where we had agreed 1,500. Then I asked what was getting in the way. He said he did not follow the regression method and was embarrassed to admit it. We agreed I would walk him through it for an hour, and he would draft in four days. He sent it in three, and it was good. We handed in on time and got the second-best mark in our group. I learned to describe what happened rather than the person, and to ask before I suggest.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: who got the feedback and what it was about
A specific situation with a real stake and a deadline
Your own actions: the setting you chose, the facts you gave and how you listened
A number or concrete result of the conversation
What you learned about giving feedback
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer gives the feedback as facts, in private, and shows that you listened. The other person should come out of the story well. Avoid a story where you only complained about someone.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you changed your mind in front of others.
widget.model: In a society trading game last spring, I reversed my own call in front of my team. We were making markets on a dice total, and I had argued hard for keeping our quotes tight. I was the team's quoter, so the call was mine. Twenty minutes in, we were short eight lots and losing about 30 points a round. A teammate said one of the bots only ever bought from us. I had dismissed that idea earlier, out loud. I checked the trade log: that bot had bought from us 14 times and sold twice. So I told the team I had been wrong, and why. I raised our offer by two and skewed both quotes up. We were flat within three rounds and finished third of twelve teams. I learned to say what evidence would change my mind before I argue, so changing it is easy.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: what you changed your mind about, and in front of whom
A specific situation where your first view carried real weight
Your own actions: the evidence you checked and how you said you were wrong
A number or concrete result after the change
What you learned about holding and changing views
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer shows the evidence that moved you and how you said so openly. Interviewers want someone who updates quickly without losing face. Keep your first view reasonable, so the change reads as judgement, not rescue.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Why do you want to be a quant researcher rather than a trader?
widget.model: I want research because the part I enjoy most is the slow question: is this effect real? Both jobs use the same maths, so the real difference is the clock. A trader decides in seconds and lives with the result that day. A researcher spends weeks testing an idea before anyone trades it, and most ideas die. Last summer I tested a simple reversal signal on five years of daily prices. The first backtest showed a Sharpe ratio of 1.8. I spent two weeks finding out why, and half of it came from stale closing prices. The honest figure was 0.6, and finding that was the best part of my summer. I also play in a society trading game, and I enjoy it. But I notice I review my trades afterwards more eagerly than I make them. Here, research feeds the traders directly, so careful work shows up in real decisions.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence with a reason, not "I like maths"
Shows what the research job involves day to day
Contrasts fairly with trading, without running it down
Evidence from your own experience, with a number
Links the reasons to this kind of firm
Under two minutes, clear, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer says what research work is and why it suits you, with evidence. Contrast it fairly with trading, since both matter at the same firm. Close by linking your reasons to the kind of firm in front of you.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: What do you do outside your studies that tells us how you think?
widget.model: I play competitive bridge, and it shows that I like deciding with half the facts and then checking myself. In bridge you see your own cards and a quarter of the others. Every bid and every card played is a small bet on what the other hands hold. I keep a notebook of every hand where I went wrong at our weekly club. Over the last year it has about 200 entries, and I tag each by cause. The biggest cause was not bad luck. It was counting the high cards too late, in about a third of my mistakes. I changed one habit: I count before my first play. My club ranking went from the middle of 40 players to the top ten. A trading desk works the same way. You act on partial information, then review honestly, and your edge comes from fixing the habits the review finds.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: the activity and the habit of thought it shows
Shows what the activity involves, concretely
Links the habit to the job fairly, without overclaiming
Evidence from your own experience, with a number
Links the habit to this kind of firm
Under two minutes, clear, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer picks one activity and names the habit of thought it trains. Back it with something you measured or changed. Link it to the work without claiming the hobby is the job.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You have thirty seconds to prepare and two minutes to answer. Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.
widget.model: The pressure I remember best was a programming exam where my code would not run with forty minutes left. The task was a small simulation worth half the marks, and I had written about 150 lines. First I stopped typing and took one minute to read the error properly. It pointed to a loop that ran one step too far. I fixed it, but the output was still wrong. Rather than rewrite everything, I tested the smallest case by hand: three steps, which I could check on paper. That showed a second bug, a sign error in one update. I fixed it with twelve minutes to spare and used the time to add comments. I scored 68% on the paper, against a class average of 55%. I learned to slow down when the clock speeds up, and to test the smallest case first.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: the pressure and what was at stake
A specific situation, set up in a few seconds
Your own actions under pressure, in order
A number or concrete result
One lesson you still use
Fits two minutes, easy to follow without notes

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: In a recorded answer, say the point in your first sentence, because nobody can ask a follow-up. Spend most of the time on what you did and in what order. Finish on time, with a result and one lesson.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: A mentor tells you that you were not chosen because you gave up too early on a final-round puzzle. How do you respond?
widget.model: I would thank her and accept it, because it matches what I remember. On the last puzzle, a dice game, I gave up after a minute and asked for a hint. I did not say what I already knew, which was most of the set-up. So I would ask her one question: was it the stopping or the silence before it? Then I would build a plan for the next round. Each week I would do ten new puzzles, five minutes each. I would keep talking for the first three minutes, whatever happens. I would record two of them and listen for the moment I go quiet. At my next final round, three months later, I would aim to give a partial answer on every question. If I stall, I would say what I would try next before asking for help.

rubric.text: Thanks the mentor and accepts the point in the first sentence, without excuses
Names the specific moment the feedback refers to
Your own actions: one question back, and a concrete practice plan
Numbers in the plan: how much, how often, how long
What you will do differently when you next stall
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer accepts the point at once and asks one sharp question about it. Then it turns the feedback into practice you can count. Never argue with the feedback or blame the interviewer.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You hold an offer that expires in 48 hours, and another firm you prefer has not replied. What do you do?
widget.model: First I would decide whether I would happily take the offer I hold, because that sets everything else. Say the offer is from a market maker. My first choice is a hedge fund that interviewed me last week. Within the first few hours I would email the fund's recruiter. I would say that my offer expires on Friday at noon, and that the fund is my first choice. I would ask whether they can tell me where I stand before then. At the same time I would call the market maker to thank them and ask for one more week. I would give an honest reason, since a decision this size deserves care. If the fund cannot answer and no extension comes, I would accept the offer I hold. Once I accept, I keep my word and withdraw elsewhere.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: the decision rule for the 48 hours
Sets out the situation: the offer in hand and the firm you prefer
Your own actions: what you tell each firm, honestly and promptly
Concrete details: the deadline, the extension asked for, the order of calls
What you do if neither firm moves, and that you keep your word
About two minutes, in order, with no filler

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong answer is honest with both firms and quick to act. Ask the slower firm for news and the faster one for time, with real dates. Never accept and then renege.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: Describe the hardest bug or analysis error in a project of yours, and how you found it.
widget.model: The hardest error I found was in my backtest of a momentum rule on 300 shares. It made the strategy look twice as good as it was. My first result was a 14% yearly return. That seemed too high for a textbook rule, so I set myself a test. I reran it on shuffled returns, where any edge should vanish. It still made 6% a year, so the code was leaking something. I could have stepped through the whole pipeline line by line, but it had 2,000 lines. Instead I checked the data after each of five stages against a hand calculation on one share. The error was in the third stage. The ranking used each day's closing price, but trades were filled at that same close. Shifting the signal by one day fixed it, and the shuffled test fell to 0.2%. The honest return was 7%. Next time I would write the shuffled test before the strategy.

rubric.text: States the project and the error in one sentence, and why it mattered
Two or more decisions you made while hunting it, each with its reason
One approach you rejected and the trade-off behind it
Numbers before and after the fix, including the disappointing one
What you would do differently
Within three minutes, ordered problem, search, fix, result

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A strong account shows how you knew something was wrong and how you narrowed the search. Give the numbers before and after the fix, even when the truth disappoints. End with the check you now run first.

items.question: Answer aloud, then write your answer here.

widget.prompt: You are halfway through an answer when the interviewer cuts in with a harder follow-up. Show me how you carry on, out loud.
widget.model: Say I am pricing a game that pays the larger of two dice, and I have just said 161/36. The interviewer cuts in: "Now three dice, and you may reroll the lowest one." First I stop and repeat the new question back, so we agree on the rules. Then I say what carries over. The larger of two dice used the chance that every die sits below a level. That trick still works for three dice. What changes is the reroll, which only matters when it can change the largest die. So I give a rough number first. Three dice without a reroll give about 4.96 for the largest. The reroll can only raise the largest die, so I expect slightly more, say just over 5. Then I commit: I will work out the exact value by conditioning on the two dice I keep. If I get stuck, I will say which step is hard.

rubric.text: Restates the new question and checks the rules before answering
Separates what carries over from the old answer from what changes
Puts a rough number down first, with a reason for its direction
Commits to a method and says it aloud, not only a process
Says what would check the estimate or show it is wrong
Thinks aloud in order, without long silences

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Interviewers interrupt to see how you handle a change, not to catch you out. Restate the new question, say what carries over, then give a rough number before the exact work. Keep talking, and say where you are stuck if you are.
